videos.script: Your provider sells you five megabits a second. Something has to hold you to it. {{contract}} There are two ways to hold traffic to a rate, and they fail in opposite ways. {{two}} A shaper keeps the packets that arrive too fast, and sends them a little later. Almost nothing is lost. Everything waits. {{shaper}} A policer does not wait. What fits the rate goes through, and the rest is thrown away on the spot. {{policer}} Both decide with the same small machine, a bucket of tokens. You will work out its numbers, and run a model of it. {{lab-shape}} Then you put a shaper on the office uplink. The upload settles, with no losses after the first second. But a ping now waits twenty-two milliseconds in its queue. {{lab-police}} Then the provider polices instead. The ping is instant again. The upload loses packets every second, more than thirteen hundred in eight. {{both}} Finally, both at once. You shape your own side just under the contract, and the provider's policer drops nothing at all. {{why}} That is the arrangement most offices want. The losses happen in your router, and the queue is yours to arrange.
